label: Telling puns and alliteration apart
subject: English

curriculumRefs.subject: English
curriculumRefs.note: alliteration is taught in the poem exercises of Unit 1

nextPractice: Spot the double meaning (pun) versus the repeated starting sound (alliteration) in short sentences.

refresher.title: Quick refresher
refresher.body: A pun is a play on words: one word (or two words that sound alike) has two meanings, and that makes it funny. Alliteration is when words close together start with the same sound. Ask yourself: is there a double meaning? Then it is a pun. Is a starting sound repeated? Then it is alliteration.

examples.label: Pun
examples.text: “I used to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough.” (dough = bread mix and money)

methods.name: Definition
methods.title: What each one means
methods.body: A pun is a play on words that uses a word with two meanings (or words that sound alike) to create humour. Alliteration is the repetition of the same starting sound in nearby words.

examples.label: Pun
examples.text: “I used to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough.” Dough is the bread mix and also a slang word for money.

examples.label: Alliteration
examples.text: “Busy bees buzz.” Three words in a row start with the b sound.

methods.name: Side-by-side comparison
methods.title: Put them side by side
methods.body: Puns are about MEANING. Alliteration is about SOUND. Check each sentence with two quick tests.
table: a word that means two things
the same first sound again and again
Can this word mean something else here?
Say the first sound of each word aloud
“The maths book looked sad because it had too many problems.”

methods.name: Picture it
methods.title: Picture it
methods.body: Imagine a pun as one word wearing two hats. In “The maths book looked sad because it had too many problems,” the word problems wears a homework hat (sums to solve) and a worry hat (troubles). Now imagine alliteration as a row of beads that are all the same colour: in “Fat frogs flop,” every bead is an f.

methods.name: Step by step
methods.title: Check it step by step
methods.body: Use these steps on any sentence.
steps: Listen to the start of each word. Do several nearby words begin with the same sound? That is alliteration.
Now look for one word that could mean two different things here. If it does, and it makes a little joke, that is a pun.
A sentence can have both. Answer the one the question asks about.

examples.label: Try it
examples.text: “The fisherman was a reel hero.” Step 3: reel (fishing reel) sounds like real. Two meanings, so it is a pun.

confusions.text: In your test, the question asked for a pun, but you chose a sentence with alliteration. Alliteration is about sounds at the start of words (“Busy bees buzz”). A pun is about meaning: one word does two jobs (“make enough dough” = bread dough and money). Look for the double meaning, not the repeated sound.

In your test, the question asked for alliteration, but you chose a sentence without a repeated starting sound. Alliteration is about sound (“Busy bees buzz”); a pun is about a word with two meanings. Say the first sound of each word aloud to check.

keyIdeas: A pun depends on a word or phrase with two meanings, or on words that sound alike but mean different things.
Alliteration is the same starting sound repeated in words that are close together.
acceptableSimpleWording: it's a joke with a word
they all start with the same letter

misconceptionRules.unlessMatches: two meanings|double meaning|means (two|2)|sounds like|other meaning|different meaning|also means
misconceptionRules.feedback: Your answer is right, but a pun is not about words starting with the same sound — that is alliteration. A pun works because a word has two meanings or sounds like another word.

misconceptionRules.reasoningMatches: two meanings|double meaning|it'?s a joke|funny|sounds like
misconceptionRules.feedback: Your answer is right, but alliteration is not about a double meaning or a joke — that is a pun. Alliteration is the same starting sound repeated in nearby words.

rubric.misconceptionFeedback: Your answer is right, but the reason mixes up the two ideas. A pun is about a word with two meanings; alliteration is about the same starting sound repeated.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a pun?
options: The bicycle couldn't stand up by itself because it was two-tired.
questions.hint: Look for a word that sounds like another word but means something different.
questions.solution: “Two-tired” sounds like “too tired”. A bicycle has two tyres, and it is also too tired to stand: one phrase, two meanings. That is a pun. “Busy birds built” repeats the b sound, which is alliteration.

whyWrong.1: “Busy birds built” repeats the b sound at the start of the words. That is alliteration, not a pun. Look for the word with two meanings instead.

questions.question: Which sentence uses alliteration?
options: I'm reading a book about glue — I can't put it down.
questions.hint: Say the first sound of each word aloud. Which sentence repeats one sound again and again?
questions.solution: “Peter's purple parrot preened proudly” repeats the p sound at the start of five words. That is alliteration. The glue sentence is a pun (“can't put it down” = it's stuck, and it's exciting).

whyWrong.0: The glue sentence is a pun: “can't put it down” means the book is stuck to your hands and also that it is exciting. Alliteration is about the same starting sound.
whyWrong.2: “The library was quiet today” has no repeated starting sound and no double meaning. Look for the sentence where the same first sound keeps coming back.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a pun?
options: The scarecrow won an award because he was outstanding in his field.
questions.hint: One of these sentences has a phrase that could mean two things for a scarecrow.
questions.solution: “Outstanding in his field” means excellent at his job, and a scarecrow really does stand out in a field. Two meanings make it a pun. “Seven slippery seals swam south” repeats the s sound: alliteration.

whyWrong.0: “Seven slippery seals swam south” repeats the s sound — that is alliteration. A pun needs a word or phrase with two meanings.

questions.question: “The tailor's business was going sew-sew.” Why is this a pun?
options: Because “sew-sew” sounds like “so-so”, and a tailor sews.
Because the words start with the same sound.
questions.hint: Say “sew-sew” aloud. What everyday word does it sound like?
questions.solution: “Sew-sew” sounds like “so-so” (not very good), and sewing is what a tailor does. A sound-alike with two meanings is a pun.

whyWrong.1: Starting sounds are what alliteration is about. This sentence is funny because “sew-sew” sounds like another word with a different meaning.
whyWrong.2: Nothing in this sentence rhymes. The joke comes from “sew-sew” sounding like “so-so”.

questions.question: “Why did the cookie go to the doctor? Because it felt crummy.” This joke uses:
questions.hint: What are crumbs? What does it mean to feel “crummy”?
questions.solution: “Crummy” means feeling unwell, and a cookie is full of crumbs. One word, two meanings: a pun.

whyWrong.0: The words in this joke don't keep starting with the same sound. The joke works because “crummy” has two meanings — that is a pun.

questions.question: Which line is alliteration, not a pun?
options: Why are fish so clever? They live in schools.
questions.hint: Which line keeps repeating one starting sound?
questions.solution: “Twelve tiny turtles tiptoed together” repeats the t sound: alliteration. The fish joke is a pun: a school of fish, and a school where you learn.

whyWrong.1: The fish line is a pun: “schools” means groups of fish and places to learn. Alliteration is the line that repeats the same starting sound.

questions.question: In “The calendar's days are numbered,” the word numbered creates a ____.
questions.hint: A calendar's days really have numbers. What else can “your days are numbered” mean?
questions.solution: A calendar's days have numbers on them, and “your days are numbered” also means something will not last long. Two meanings: a pun.
questions.wrongFeedback: “Numbered” works in two ways here: the dates on a calendar have numbers, and “days are numbered” means time is running out. A word with two meanings makes a pun.

questions.question: “Daring dolphins dive deep” repeats the d sound at the start of words. This is called ____.
questions.hint: It is the name for repeating the same starting sound in nearby words. It starts with “a”.
questions.solution: Repeating the same starting sound in nearby words is called alliteration: daring, dolphins, dive, deep.
questions.wrongFeedback: When the same starting sound is repeated in words close together, it is called alliteration.

questions.question: “I'm on a seafood diet — I see food and I eat it.” Because “seafood” and “see food” sound alike but mean different things, this joke is a ____.
questions.hint: Sound-alike words with different meanings are the key to this kind of joke.
questions.solution: “Seafood” (fish) and “see food” (any food you can see) sound the same but mean different things. That is a pun.
questions.wrongFeedback: The joke depends on two words that sound the same but mean different things — that makes it a pun.

questions.question: “Lucky lions leap loudly” is an example of ____.
questions.hint: Say the first sound of each word: l, l, l, l.
questions.solution: Every word starts with the l sound. Repeating a starting sound like this is alliteration.
questions.wrongFeedback: All four words start with the l sound. Repeating the starting sound in nearby words is called alliteration.

questions.question: “Never trust an atom — they make up everything.” “Make up” has two meanings here, so the sentence is a ____.
questions.hint: Atoms make up (form) everything. What else can “make up” mean?
questions.solution: Atoms make up (form) everything, and to “make up” a story means to invent it. Two meanings: a pun.
questions.wrongFeedback: “Make up” means to form something and also to invent a story. A phrase with two meanings creates a pun.
